lessons.title: Why Producers and Consumers Hedge — Real Indian Examples

children.text: According to data compiled by the Gem & Jewellery Export Promotion Council, the average international gold price jumped from about $3,242 per troy ounce in April to May 2025 to about $4,724 per troy ounce in the same months of 2026, a rise of nearly 46% in one year. A jewellery exporter who had quoted export prices to an overseas buyer months in advance, based on the earlier, lower gold price, would have watched input costs run far ahead of revenue on that order, unless they had locked in their gold cost using futures. This is not a hypothetical. It is the everyday reality that makes hedging a genuine business decision for some Indian companies, and, just as tellingly, a decision some large companies deliberately choose not to make.

body.text: Hedging trades away an uncertain outcome, which could be better or worse than expected, for a known, plannable one. It makes sense exactly when unhedged price swings threaten a business's core economics, and it can make just as much sense to skip if a business has a cheaper way to manage that same risk.

children.text: Producers: Farmers and FPOs Selling Ahead

A farmer who has already sown a crop cannot control what it sells for at harvest, only how much of that risk to carry alone. Since 2016, NCDEX has run a dedicated platform connecting Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) to its futures market, and by now several hundred FPOs across roughly a dozen states have used it to hedge price risk across around 17 commodities. One documented case is a Saurashtra-based FPO in Gujarat, which, after training on the platform, executed its first hedge trade in May 2018. NCDEX also runs an early pay-in facility: an FPO that deposits its produce into an exchange-approved warehouse right after taking a sell position is exempted from most margin requirements, needing to fund only mark-to-market movements, which makes hedging far more accessible for a cash-strapped farmer collective.
Here is the mechanics in a simplified example, ignoring basis risk for now (Lesson 3 of this chapter deals with that complication in full):
An FPO expects to harvest and sell 100 quintals of jeera in three months. Worried about a bumper crop pushing prices down by then, it sells (goes short) jeera futures today at ₹21,500 per quintal.

body.caption: The FPO's hedge, three months later

cells: Futures sold at ₹21,500, now settling near ₹18,800: a gain of about ₹2,700/quintal
Futures sold at ₹21,500, now settling near ₹24,000: a loss of about ₹2,500/quintal

body.text: Notice what the hedge actually did in both rows: it locked in roughly ₹21,500 per quintal either way. The FPO gave up the chance to benefit from a price spike in exchange for protection against a price crash. That trade-off, not a guaranteed profit, is the entire point of hedging.

children.text: Processors and Manufacturers: Locking In Input Costs

MCX gold futures are widely used by bullion importers and jewellery manufacturers precisely because gold is their largest single input cost. Consider a jewellery exporter who has just confirmed an overseas order requiring 1 kg of gold, to be sourced and shipped in two months. Gold today (illustrative figures) is at ₹60,000 per 10 grams, meaning the raw material alone will cost ₹60,00,000 at today's price. Rather than leave that cost exposed to a possible repeat of the kind of surge GJEPC's data showed over the last year, the exporter buys (goes long) 1 lot of MCX Gold futures at ₹60,000 per 10 grams.

body.caption: The exporter's hedge, two months later

cells: Long futures at ₹60,000, settling near ₹66,000: a gain of ₹6,00,000
Long futures at ₹60,000, settling near ₹55,000: a loss of ₹5,00,000

body.text: Look closely at the second row. The exporter's hedge cost them ₹5,00,000 in the scenario where gold got cheaper, because they had already given up that potential saving to protect against the opposite outcome. A hedger who complains about 'losing money on the futures position' when prices moved in their favour on the physical side has misunderstood what they signed up for.

children.text: The Company That Chooses Not to Hedge: A Tale of Three Airlines

Aviation turbine fuel (ATF) typically makes up 40% of an Indian airline's operating costs, and can climb to 60% during a sharp price spike. If any industry should hedge fuel aggressively, it should be this one. And yet India's three largest listed carriers have taken three different approaches.

body.title: Three airlines, three fuel risk strategies

columns.label: IndiGo: minimal financial hedging
points: India's largest airline by market share generally does not hedge jet fuel through derivatives
Relies instead on an operational hedge: a short 30-to-45-day booking cycle lets it reprice fares quickly as fuel costs move
Scale and a low-cost structure give it room to absorb short-term fuel swings that smaller rivals cannot

columns.label: Air India: episodic hedger
points: Began hedging fuel in 2002, then discontinued the programme within a few years
Resumed hedging around 2015, at one point covering roughly a fifth of its annual fuel consumption
Its approach has shifted with management, ownership and market views over time

columns.label: SpiceJet: modest, growing hedge
points: Hedges only a small share of consumption, historically around 5%
Has stated intentions to raise that share meaningfully over time
Reflects a middle path between IndiGo's near-total reliance on pass-through and a large, standing hedge programme

body.text: This is the single most important idea in this lesson: hedging is a choice, not an obligation, and it is not free. IndiGo effectively substitutes an operational hedge, the ability to pass costs to customers within weeks, for a financial one. That works for a dominant, low-cost carrier with pricing power. A weaker competitor with less pricing power and thinner margins may reasonably decide it cannot afford to be unhedged in the same way. Neither choice is automatically wrong.

children.text: Exporters and Importers: When Currency Meets Commodity

A textile exporter who has quoted a price to a European buyer in dollars, based on today's cotton cost, faces the same exposure as the jewellery exporter above, except the raw material this time is cotton rather than gold. An importer of base metals for a manufacturing unit faces the mirror image of the FPO's problem: a price rise between order and delivery erodes their margin the same way a price fall erodes a farmer's. The direction of the exposure differs by business, but the underlying discipline is identical: identify what you are already exposed to, then decide, deliberately, whether and how much of it to hedge.

body.title: Should this business hedge?
body.scenario: A mid-sized Coimbatore-based spinning mill buys raw cotton continuously and sells finished yarn on 60-day payment terms to garment exporters at prices agreed at the time of order. Cotton costs are around 55% of the mill's total production cost, and the mill operates on thin, single-digit margins. It currently does not hedge its cotton purchases.
body.prompt: Using the reasoning from the airline comparison above, would you recommend this mill start hedging its cotton exposure with MCX or NCDEX cotton futures? What about its situation makes the case one way or the other?
body.modelAnswer: The case for hedging is strong here, more like Air India or SpiceJet's situation than IndiGo's. The mill has a large cost exposure to a single volatile input (cotton at 55% of production cost), thin margins that leave little room to absorb a price spike, and no obvious operational hedge equivalent to IndiGo's short booking cycle, since it has already agreed prices with its garment-exporter customers before delivery. Unlike a dominant, pricing-power-rich company that can pass costs through quickly, this mill's margin is directly at the mercy of the gap between its cotton purchase price and its already-fixed yarn selling price. A reasonable recommendation would be to hedge at least the portion of cotton purchases tied to already-quoted yarn orders.

cards.definition: A non-financial way of managing price risk, such as a short pricing or booking cycle that lets a business pass on cost changes quickly, used as a substitute or complement to hedging with derivatives.
A hedge taken by someone who will sell a commodity later (like a farmer), typically done by selling (going short) futures to lock in a selling price.
A hedge taken by someone who will buy a commodity later (like a jewellery manufacturer), typically done by buying (going long) futures to lock in a purchase price.
An NCDEX facility letting an FPO deposit produce into an approved warehouse right after taking a sell position, reducing the margin it must fund to mark-to-market only.

points: Hedging is a deliberate trade-off: giving up potential upside to protect against downside, not a guaranteed way to make money.
Producers like farmers and FPOs typically hedge by selling futures to lock in a future selling price; NCDEX's FPO platform, running since 2016, has helped hundreds of FPOs do exactly this.
Processors and manufacturers, such as jewellery exporters, typically hedge by buying futures to lock in a future purchase cost, especially when the input is a large share of total cost.
Hedging is a choice, not an obligation. IndiGo, Air India and SpiceJet show three genuinely different, and each individually rational, approaches to the same jet fuel exposure.
The right question is never 'should every business always hedge?' but 'given this specific business's margins, cost structure and ability to pass on price changes, does hedging make sense here?'

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Company-specific hedging practices mentioned here are drawn from public reporting and can change; they illustrate general principles rather than current, guaranteed policy. Numeric examples use illustrative prices.
